newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African maize prices ease despite harvest delay.
newsitem.headline: S.African maize prices ease despite harvest delay.

text.p: Prices for South African maize, the country's most important farming commodity, are trending weaker despite a supply squeeze sparked by a delay in this season's harvest and exports of white grain to Kenya.

Industry sources said on Monday that expectations of a bumper U.S. crop later this year and a belief that the local harvest will begin in earnest this month after unseasonally wet and cold weather in May, was keeping bids and offers down.
Other price-depressing factors in the 1997 maize year (May-April) was a forecast surplus of between one and two million tonnes of local maize and the threat of cheap global imports, they said.
"Prices are still trending downwards especially in the later months," said Rod Blondin, general manager of the agricultural markets division of the South African Futures Exchange.

At 1300 GMT white maize contracts for July delivery were bid at 570.00 rand a tonne, down from peaks of around 670 rand in February. Yellow July maize was bid at 545.00 rand, also well down on highs of near 700 rand in February.
"The bottom is already starting to fall out of the market with the very good news for the U.S. crop," said one physical maize trader.

"Ex-silo for (spot) white we are paying between 570 and 580 rand a tonne, and for yellow a little less. But looking ahead at 30-day maize it is at around 480. And after June we are looking at prices being much lower," he said.
Latest forecasts by the International Grains Council peg the U.S. 1997 maize crop at a massive 277.1 million tonnes, its second highest ever following good weather conditions and increased sowings.
South Africa's National Maize Producers Organisation (Nampo) said last week that the South African harvest was proceeding very slowly despite the return of dry weather after heavy rains in late May.

Local traders said last week that white maize was being exported to Kenya following a drought which has created food shortages throughout the East African region. Although initial quantities are small at around 70,000 tonnes, more maize has been earmarked for the region.

The National Crop Estimates Committee has estimated a 1997 commercial crop of some 7.660 million tonnes, which although two million tonnes below last year's big harvest, is well above consumption needs.
